title: Tenstorrent hits $6.2B valuation to scale open-weight AI chips
snippet: After drawing acquisition interest earlier this year, the Nvidia challenger raised $1.5 billion to remain independent.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

11:37 AM PDT · October 19, 2026

Image Credits:Tenstorrent

		

							

											
									

					

	

Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation. The round comes five months after the 10-year-old Nvidia challenger reportedly received acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations of as much as $5 billion.

The fresh round, which more than doubled Tenstorrent’s valuation from the $2.6 billion it fetched in late 2024, was led by Trace Capital, a new firm launched by Quiet Capital co-founder Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X. Other backers included Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price.

Jim Keller, a prominent microprocessor engineer and Tenstorrent CEO, told Bloomberg that the company decided to remain independent and raise more capital after it showed that its Galaxy servers could run DeepSeek models. The new capital will go toward scaling chips tailored for serving open-weight AI models and video generation.

Tenstorrent is part of a wave of AI hardware startups trying to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance. Among them is Etched, an AI chip maker that was fielding investment offers at valuations of $40 billion or more, TechCrunch reported earlier this month.

title: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life
snippet: AI companion app Tolan has raised another $30 million after attracting more than 250,000 active users.
fullText:
Tolan, the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital.

The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by Upstarts Media. (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but PitchBook estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”)

Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos.

Image Credits:Tolan on App Store

Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is now in the “double-digit millions.” 

The startup is one of the few AI companions that have found some traction, as it claims to have more than 250,000 active users who have had more than 70 million conversations over the past year. Around 70% of its users are women, and 40% are parents, Tolan’s team told the news outlet. (Anecdotally, the app is said to appeal in particular to neurodivergent people, who may benefit from additional support, whether that’s emotional support or help with organizing tasks.)

Compared with other companions, Tolan seems to have found a balance between being helpful without being perceived as too weird. Compare that with the public shaming that Friend’s pendant-based AI companion faced; users dubbed Friend “very cringe,” The New York Times called it “hated,” and Wired said it “has no soul.”

Meanwhile, another former top contender in the space, Character.AI, recently filed for bankruptcy after its founder’s return to Google. (Its remaining staff is transitioning to Disney, which bought some of its assets.)

However, Tolan could end up facing increased competition from the more recent crop of AI agents, which help users plan, organize, and accomplish their tasks and goals, not just talk their way through them. For instance, Meta gave its AI agent Muse a cute avatar for its users to talk to, which it also plans to release as a hardware product in the future.

The startup also has to navigate the risks of offering AI-powered emotional support, given that multiple lawsuits have been filed against general-purpose AI app makers alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to users’ suicides.

title: Voicemod’s New Phone Gadget Changes Your ‘Sonic Identity’ for Mobile Games and Streaming
snippet: Clip it to the back of your phone, and it’ll convert your voice on the fly for fun, privacy and accessibility.
fullText:
For years, Voicemod has given people a way to change their voices online, which they’ve done for any number of benign reasons — for game players with feminine-pitched voices to avoid harassment, for those with damaged vocal cords to simulate their former voices, for anonymity or even just for fun. Now the company has a new product to bring its voice-changing tech on the go in a physical device that magnetically clips on the back of phones.

The Voicemod Key Pocket, available to preorder now for $130, is a small soundboard about the size of a magnetic battery and serves as a controller interface for the company’s voice-changing apps. The half-dozen buttons on the back of the device can be used to switch between voices or audio effects while streaming or playing games, while the wheel adjusts volume of the projected voice. 

The Key Pocket works in tandem with the Voicemod app, but all voice processing is done locally and in real time separate from games and streaming apps in order to maximize privacy as well as performance, according to a Voicemod statement. The Voicemod app provides access to over 200 original voices made by the company, over 76,000 voices made by the service’s community and over 800,000 sounds and memes made by users. 

			

More from CNET

The Key Pocket is a versatile gizmo, with an LED wheel at the top-left corner for toggling voices and checking sound setup, while programmable trigger buttons enable swapping between voices and soundboard playback. The device supports wired and Bluetooth wireless headsets, has USB passthrough charging and clips securely to the back of phones with MagSafe-compatible magnets. 

Beyond phones, the Key Pocket works on tablets and consoles, including PS4 and PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2 and the Meta Quest 2, 3 and 3S headsets. It can plug into USB-C, wired 3.5mm ports or connect via Bluetooth.

There are plenty of reasons folks might want to change their voice, from goofing off with friends to avoiding harassment when gaming online — a sad reality for gamers with feminine voices. It’s also an accessibility boon for people who have health conditions or other circumstances leading them to want to change their vocal timbre and pitch.

These days, changing voices can be cause for concern, especially with artificial-intelligence scams spoofing the voices of loved ones to extort money. But when I sat down at Mobile World Congress 2026 earlier this year to chat with Voicemod’s Daniel Pearson, vice president of marketing, and Alex Bordanova, chief product and technology officer, they explained how it aligned with the ethos of the company. The Key Pocket is the result of years of Voicemod’s work to support the idea that one’s online voice is as much an expression of identity as their visual look.

“Everyone has their digital visual appearance where they tweak their cosmetics and skins, but when it comes to voice, it’s kind of been left out, right? It’s this missing half of digital identity,” said Pearson. 

As voice-changing tech makes its way into Fortnite, Arc Raiders, Marvel Rivals and other spaces for online third spaces, people are opening up to the idea that their personal expression isn’t just limited to how they’re seen, but also how they’re heard — or as Pearson calls it, their “sonic identity.”

Voicemod

When voice becomes a way to express identity

In our earlier chat, Pearson and Bordanova laid out what Voicemod meant to its community, with the latter describing one memorable story from last October’s TwitchCon 2025. A woman approached him explaining that she was a streamer who lost her voice for about six months but was able to make up for it with Voicemod’s tech.

“She used an AI voice, because that was enough to turn something audible out of just very nuanced sounds that she could project,” Bordanova said. 

It spurred discussion about ways the Voicemod team might preserve the community’s voices — a vault, say, to future-proof their voices in the event that health or injury might limit their speaking. 

The Voicemod creators don’t just see its tech as just to alter voices for fun or privacy — they see it as an expression machine, one that reflects who you are online. That comes in the form of a voice tweaked to a desired pitch and timbre, but also more abstract communication, like a soundboard. Yes, the signature toy of radio shock jocks from yesteryear is an aspect of expression, too, especially among a community where sounds take on specific meanings.

“It’s giving you the capacity to react and expand by giving extra context that you and your friends understand, but the normies don’t,” said Pearson.

Voicemod’s team has been encouraged by the increasing availability of voice-changing tech in games. Around a year ago, Arc Raiders launched its voice changer in beta but only offered ten voices at launch, and Voicemod offered their own tech to expand those options. 

“[Gamers] are social beings, they don’t want to have the default skin. They want to have their own skin customized,” Pearson said. “If the game just gives you 5-10 skins, you’re gonna want the next one, you want to differentiate yourself.”

The company’s Voicelab enables further voice tweaking with fun effects. One could, if they wanted, change their voice to sound like they were wearing a helmet in a cave inside a volcano — wacky but evocative sonic context placing the person in a specific space and circumstance. It enhances expression and storytelling and uses AI to do it. But not the AI you’re thinking of.

AI has been at the heart of Voicemod — but not generative AI

There’s no denying that technological advancement has enabled voice generation, but Voicemod came long before that. It was founded 14 years ago, using digital sound processing to alter voices, launching first on an iPhone 3GS, Bordanova explained. 

What their tech enabled that traditional DSP could not is changing the timbre of the voice — its tone, color and personality. Using math, Voicemod’s tech could change a vocal signal in ways that would simulate changing the human organs that naturally shape one’s voice, like elongating or shrinking the vocal cords or altering the width of your throat or nose. 

More traditional AI powered Voicemod’s older methods of voice changing, which improved thanks to technological developments. The company’s advantage was to be one of the first to invest heavily in AI’s use in voice changing, Bordanova said. 

“There was something unique, something very special, that would evolve us from being a voice changer to having fun with friends online, into giving real utility for a 24/7 use case,” Bordanova said. 

What he clarifies is that Voicemod’s tech isn’t based on generative AI, unlike the tech behind voice processing tricks like Google’s live translation. Instead, their language models are around 20 megabytes in weight, and take about a week to train. Unlike the immense large language models used in generative AI, Voicemod’s are small enough to fully download on phones and other client-side devices. They can be consulted immediately on device for 42 millisecond latency, rather than need to go to the cloud.

That doesn’t mean they’ll never use LLMs — but the use case they’re envisioning is as a glorified assistant helping people find the right toggles and settings to get the voice they want from existing choices. 

“You can type, I want the voice of SpongeBob and the LLM would pick the right effect and parameters and just create the voice for us,” Bordanova said. 

Voicemod

Expression on the go, through your phone to your digital life

Back in March at MWC 2026, I chatted with Bordanova and Pearson when they brought out a prototype for the Key Pocket, the follow-up to the company’s earlier Voicemod Key, a dongle device that aimed to help change voices for console play. Even in its cruder form, the Key Pocket felt special. 

As even the prototype was MagSafe compatible, I clipped it to the back of my own iPhone 15 Pro Max. Even if the device wasn’t far enough along to be usable with software, I could still simulate how it would feel in action with my phone rotated sideways, as if I had it active while gaming. The row of buttons rested below my fingers, easy to press if I wanted to tweak my voice or trigger vocal or sound effects. The volume wheel was nice and accessible. If I was streaming or chatting with my friends, the Key Pocket would be a nice accessory to have.

While a lot of gaming happens at home on PC and console, mobile gaming is a huge sector. The Key Pocket is a neat tool for gamers who either play on the go or who opt to play on phones for other reasons — possibly because they can’t afford pricey bigger platforms, which have only gotten more expensive since the RAM shortage. Odds are good that the phone in many gamers’ pockets can play the games they want, and the Key Pocket could help with their so-called sonic identity.

Voicemod’s goal goes beyond the Key Pocket to eventually integrate their tech at a system level, so that anyone booting up a computer or phone could use the tens of thousands of voices created by the Voicemod community (along with the filters and sound effects) to modify their aural appearance anywhere on the device. 

“The last frontier is to get rid of the hardware,” Bordanova said.

Expanding Voicemod’s tech across a device’s software and apps would broaden its appeal — imagine not just customizing your voice in games and voice chats with friends, but work Zooms and other calls. Having the same options and interface available everywhere you could use your voice would open up possibilities for folks who’ve never thought about tweaking their voices.

But any mobile gamer will tell you that external controls make a world of difference compared to on-screen digital buttons. Integrating voice tech into the back end of devices is good, but having the Key Pocket soundboard at the touch of your fingers is a far more tactile and responsive set of controls. For streamers and presenters on the go who rely on exact timing, the Key Pocket is a neat solution. Sometimes all you need is an attractively designed gadget to expose folks to new tech possibilities — and in this case, the potential to express themselves online in a way they may not have considered before.

title: Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers
snippet: Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation. more…
fullText:
Google hands out extended free trials to its AI Pro subscription frequently with new smartphone purchases and more, but trial users end up getting less access compared to paid subscribers in what is a bit of a misleading situation.

Free trials are a pretty standard practice across the industry when it comes to subscriptions, and the general understanding is that you’re getting full access to the same subscription you are later set to pay for unless there’s an upfront stipulation about restrictions.

And that’s where things are getting a bit messy with Google’s AI Pro subscription.

Google One AI Pro is a $19.99/month subscription that delivers access to expanded Gemini usage limits, 5TB of storage across Google products, and bundles in other subscriptions such as Google Home Premium, Health Premium, and YouTube Premium Lite. Earlier this year, we called AI Pro “one of the best deals in tech today.”

	

But the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon to Google’s Antigravity development tool put a spotlight on a restriction on AI Pro’s free trials. Put simply, they’re limited compared to paid subscribers, and it’s not something Google made abundantly clear.

There are two specific downsides with a Google One AI Pro trial compared to an actively paid subscription. As mentioned, Antigravity on AI Pro trials leaves out Gemini 4 Argon. Google has a page that specifically puts a trial account in a completely different bucket compared to a paid AI Pro plan, and it treats the trial as a free user with expanded usage limits rather than a full user as @evowizz was one of the first to point out.

The other restriction is YouTube Premium Lite, which is not available for Google One AI Pro trial users until they start paying.

In Google’s defense, this is technically spelled out on support documents. The YouTube Premium Lite restriction, for example, is clearly spelled out as Google says that the “benefit is unavailable until trials of Google AI Pro conclude and you convert to a paid subscription.” But, as far as we can see, this is not disclosed as clearly at the time of sign-up or alongside advertising of the AI Pro trials.

Another loss here is the lack of Google One’s 10% cashback (store credit) perk in the Google Store, which is lacking in free trials. That one is certainly easier to see the reasoning behind, though.

The Google Store touts the Pixel 11’s AI Pro trial as delivering “expanded usage limits in Gemini, access to Gemini in Google apps, and 5 TB of cloud storage,” as well as Health Premium. Nowhere does Google promise the YouTube perks, but the wording around Gemini also lacks any hint at the restriction found in Antigravity. Pages including offer details also lack any mention of this.

As mentioned, Google hands out free, extended trials to AI Pro all over the place. Just a few active examples include:

6 months free with the purchase of a Pixel 11

12 months free with the purchase of a Googlebook

6 months free for select Verizon customers

12 months free with Chromebook Plus or 3 months with any other Chromebook

6 months free with the purchase of a Galaxy Z Fold 8

And that’s just a few examples – you can absolutely find more.

	

Google explicitly lists all of these trials at their full monthly value (i.e. $119 value for Pixel’s 6-month trial) despite the restricted access that trial users see.

While Google has not addressed the somewhat misleading nature of the AI Pro trial restrictions, one Googler responded to the other headache that exists here – you can’t just press a button to start paying for AI Pro if you’re on a trial. You either have to wait for the trial to end, or reach out to Google for help converting your account. 

What do you think of the situation?

title: YouTube’s contextual AI search rolls out to all users on Android and iOS in US
snippet: “Ask YouTube” is no longer a YouTube Premium feature as the conversational AI search becomes available on mobile Android and iOS devices. more…
fullText:
“Ask YouTube” is no longer a YouTube Premium feature as the conversational AI search becomes available on mobile Android and iOS devices.

Today, Google announced the Ask YouTube feature would be widely rolling out to mobile users, in addition to TV instances of the YouTube app. Unlike before, Ask YouTube will now be accessible to all users, not just Premium subscribers. 

Access to some form of contextual AI model has been available on YouTube for a while, dating back to 2023. Since then, Google has settled on an “Ask YouTube” button that lets users ask questions about videos to get more insight. The rollout has been limited, with TVs and Premium users getting access first.

The feature has evolved a bit, and it’s taken on a conversation-oriented presentation. It isn’t limited to questions about the video or what happens at which timestamp. It’s powered through Gemini, so its answers go beyond strictly what’s in the video you’re watching.

	

Google also notes that users will be able to use Ask YouTube from the watch page in their Shorts feed and during live streams, but that feature will be a later release. For the time being, users in the US can expect Ask YouTube to show up on your mobile Android or iOS device soon as it rolls out to more users. Google says it plans to gradually expand availability.

Americans have a privacy problem, and that shouldn’t surprise anyone. Between the unprecedented backlash around Flock cameras and, more quietly, data brokers selling off our identities, individual privacy is center stage right now. I would go as far as to make it the inaugural Security Bite ‘Theme of the Year.’

Yet despite all of that, a new survey from data removal service Incogni found that 45% of the 1,517 U.S. adults polled say they aren’t concerned about their online privacy. That wasn’t even the best part of this survey though…

Among people who said they have nothing to hide, 58% would refuse to hand a stranger their unlocked phone for any amount of money, 39% cover the camera on their phone or laptop, and nearly half wouldn’t hand over their text messages to the government or “Big Tech,” even for three months of their income.

I asked Ron Zayas, founder and CEO of Ironwall by Incogni, what’s actually going on here, and he basically replied that privacy only feels abstract until it isn’t.

“We take privacy for granted, until it means that someone will read our messages, charge us more, put us in danger or disclose intimate details about us,” he told me. “But the reality is, all of that is privacy.” He also thinks companies lean on that gap on purpose, pointing out that if a privacy policy actually said “download this app and we will go through your contacts, suck in your photos, analyze your habits and share those details with anyone willing to pay us,” most of us would pause. Instead, they open with “we value your privacy” and bury the rest in legalese.

The survey also found that 65% of respondents have no idea how many websites they’re registered on, and honestly, I’m not sure I could tell you mine either. We’ve all spent the last decade or so creating accounts for things we used once and forgot about, and every one of them is still holding onto something. You can’t protect data you don’t remember giving away, right?

So I asked Zayas where someone on an iPhone or Mac should start if they want to cut that down without going full underground, and his answer was more Apple-friendly than I was expecting. “Apple has some pretty good safety protocols, much better than Google in my opinion, and makes them far easier to access,” he said. “Turn off as much of ad personalization, location sharing and contact sharing as you can. It only takes a moment.” He also recommends treating your phone number like you would a credit card number. Allowing an app to have access to your contacts will also give it your own.

Zayas put it well when he said that believing you have to “go full bunker in Montana” to have any privacy is a fallacy companies push to make people feel helpless, and I agree with him. If you live in California, the CCPA and Delete Act let you force a good chunk of your data off the market for free. For everyone else, a few minutes to clean things up in Privacy & Security can go a long way. The survey honestly put it better by saying, most of us already act like our privacy matters, so we might as well stop saying it doesn’t.

title: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
snippet: OpenCode is an open source AI coding agent that's become a popular alternative to Claude Code and Cursor. But hackers got into part of its online platform and stole some users’ API keys, and the AI tools it turned to for help kept refusing to look at the malicious code.
fullText:
OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent that has been gaining ground among developers as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight, affecting 1.4% of users of its online platform, OpenCode Console, where some users store the API keys, or digital passwords, they use to access AI services.

As the OpenCode team struggled to keep pace with the attack, the scramble to respond highlighted a growing problem: Companies without vetted access to AI models with fewer safety restrictions have a hard time defending against large-scale, AI-driven cyberattacks.

“We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the company wrote on X. “We have notified them all this morning via email.” Users who did not receive an email were not impacted, the company said.

While the company didn’t specify how the distillation attack occurred, leaked API keys can help users in countries with restricted access to American models generate the high volume of outputs needed for that process. Some skeptics called the framing an overstretch, arguing that the incident was a straightforward breach whose use for distillation remains unproven.

Overnight, developers began posting spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X: “I saw my Open AI, Anthropic, and Google AI spend alerts all fire off before going to bed wondering what was going on,” a developer wrote. 

Other users reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on individual accounts; a few described totals above $1,000.

Anthropic and Google both blocked the API keys they believed were exposed, while OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode said refunds for unauthorized charges are underway.

The exposed keys were confined to Console, where some users had them in workspaces. The open source app and command-line tool were not affected, according to co-founder Dax Raad. “Note this is the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself, those keys never come to us,” he wrote on X.

Even as users and AI companies moved to disable the exposed keys, the OpenCode team was still under pressure. Raad said attackers had been trying to break into its systems nonstop for 48 hours, requiring the team to keep AI defensive agents running around the clock. AI models that the OpenCode team turned to for analysis helped for a while, but started refusing to work when the malicious code they were asked to examine activated safety filters. 

“[T]hat was a bit frustrating,” he wrote on X.

OpenCode later received access to OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users AI models that are less likely to refuse requests for defensive security work. Raad said the access improved the team’s ability to investigate the attack.

OpenCode isn’t the first company to hit this wall. In July, AI platform Hugging Face said commercial AI models blocked its attempts to analyze activity logs from an intrusion by autonomous AI agents, which OpenAI later revealed were its own models running with safeguards lowered during a test. In a section of its blog post titled “The asymmetry problem,” Hugging Face wrote that guardrails “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” 

Security researchers have raised similar complaints, saying the restrictions are inconsistent and have pushed some toward foreign open-weight models, which anyone can download and run.

The weekend episode drew a response from David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

“OpenCode (and earlier Hugging Face) hit the same wall mid-attack: frontier models refused to analyze the very exploits needed for defense because the payloads tripped safety filters. The guardrails backfired,” he wrote on X.

The breach occurred the same night OpenCode made GLM-5.3-Flash free for users. The broader GLM-5.3 family has drawn attention from researchers who study open-weight models and note that its cybersecurity capabilities approached levels previously associated with restricted-access models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview. 

OpenCode has not detailed how attackers gained access to the older system, how keys were stored, or the full extent of any misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. The company said the incident remains ongoing.

The breach lands amid a run of AI-enabled cyber incidents. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said a China-based hacker likely used an AI penetration-testing agent, which probes computer systems for weaknesses, and Claude in attacks on South Korean banks. Last week, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that AI agents, including some being tested by AI companies, had reached Indian organizations’ systems without authorization.

title: Gemini AI Plus subscribers will lose access to Pro models next month
snippet: Google has begun emailing Gemini AI Plus members to inform them when their Gemini subscription will no longer include access to the advanced models – just Flash. more…
fullText:
Google has begun emailing Gemini AI Plus members to inform them when their Gemini subscription will no longer include access to the advanced models – just Flash.

A change in Gemini’s subscription model was announced earlier this month. It came right before Google’s new Argon model went live and became the new high-performance offer in Gemini. The company made it clear that Gemini 4 Argon would be included for AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers, but it also said AI Plus members would lose access to AI Pro entirely.

According to one user on Reddit, Google has begun emailing AI Plus subscribers to let them know Gemini Pro models would be excluded from the AI Plus tier starting on November 13. The email lists Flash-Lite and Flash as the only two options after that date.

We wanted to let you know about changes to the models that you can access with your Google AI Plus plan.

Starting on ﻿1﻿3﻿ ﻿N﻿o﻿v﻿e﻿m﻿b﻿e﻿r﻿ ﻿2﻿0﻿2﻿6﻿, the ability to select Pro models in both the Gemini app and AI Mode in Google Search will only be available to Google AI Pro subscribers and above. You’ll still have access to our latest Flash-Lite model and Flash, built for speed and intelligence. Your previous chats using the Pro model can be continued with a different model.

To learn more about these changes, you can visit our Help Centre article for additional details. You can manage or cancel your subscription at any time.

Thank you for being a Google AI Plus subscriber.

– The Google One team

A couple of others report getting the same email, which puts a pin on exactly when the Gemini AI Plus plan changes.

	

The $4.99/month option will give users access to just two models, while the $19.99/month tier gains access to Argon, leaving a bigger gap between the two. Google is still keeping the free plan around, which leaves everyone with access to Flash-lite.

Of course, these subscriptions tie into Google Workspace for cloud storage and other perks, like YouTube Premium. Still, the $4.99/month plan seemed like a good deal for those who wanted access to more capable models for more than just passive chats.

title: Data Centers Are Burning Fossil Fuels. It’s Destroying Big Tech’s Climate Goals
snippet: In his new book, Paris Marx explores how global anti-data center movements are fighting Big Tech’s power over us.
fullText:
From Ashburn, Virginia, to South Dublin, Ireland, the data centers that journalist Paris Marx visited all looked remarkably similar: large industrial facilities with loud air-conditioning units running to keep racks upon racks of servers cool. But it was the security measures around the data centers that struck Marx more than anything. 

Tall fences. Security cameras everywhere. Locks on every door that required one of the few full-time employees to unlock with a badge. And in one memorable instance, standing on an Irish public curb outside a cluster of Microsoft-owned centers, there was an eerie feeling of being watched by men on lawn mowers, trimming grass that clearly didn’t need to be cut.

“It was just really staggering to me that it was at that level that it was so hard to move through these spaces,” Marx told me.

			

More from CNET

The intense security should give you an idea of just how serious Big Tech is about its data centers. These facilities are the key to the artificial intelligence programs at OpenAI, Meta, Google, Amazon and elsewhere, creating vast amounts of compute and sucking up equally staggering amounts of electricity and water. 

There is no stronger metaphor for the manifestation of Big Tech’s power than the increasing sprawl of data centers. Amazon, Microsoft and Google alone control 59% of hyperscale data center capacity. In his new book available now, Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires, Marx, host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast, highlights how global data center protests are one of many ways that communities are pushing back against Big Tech’s power over us.

Hyperscale demands

Data centers existed long before generative AI; we called them server farms, and they’re what keep us online. But in this AI era, we have hyperscale data centers.

Before, a large data center might require around 50 megawatts of power to keep everything running. Now, hyperscale data centers can require triple that amount of power. Newer ones, like Meta’s Louisiana data center, may require 4,500 megawatts (4.5 gigawatts) — staggering demand that officials say is four times more than all of the electricity used in New Orleans on its hottest day in 2025. It’s more than the two gigawatts the Hoover Dam produces.

Hyperscale data centers are also housing more advanced tech. Chips like GPUs are key to creating compute, and newer chips built for AI data centers can run hotter. That makes it even harder to cool facilities, so in addition to air conditioning, facilities are using water systems to avoid servers overheating. It’s an additional environmental toll. A hyperscale center can suck up 1 million to 5 million gallons of water every day, equivalent to a town of more than 10,000 residents, according to a 2025 estimate.

So how do you keep these facilities running? The process to get approved and connected to a town’s electrical grid can take years. So tech companies have started building their own power plants right next to data centers for the sole purpose of keeping them on — perfect for burning massive amounts of fossil fuels, the main contributor to the climate crisis.

Hyperscale impacts

In the 2010s, Amazon, Microsoft, Google and many others pledged some version of becoming carbon neutral (or negative) in the next few decades — meaning they would offset the emissions they created with at least as much emission-reducing actions. 

Sustainability reports from that time show that, overall, tech companies were measurably decreasing their environmental footprint. “And then ChatGPT comes along, and all of a sudden, that’s out the window,” Marx told me.

Tech leaders have been candid about allowing generative AI to override their climate goals. Google reported a 50% increase in its greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 to support its generative AI. Microsoft’s pledge to be carbon negative by 2030 “was before the explosion in artificial intelligence,” Brad Smith, the company’s president, told Bloomberg in 2023, saying the carbon goal was “five times as far away as it was in 2020” because of AI. 

Modern data centers and their power plants burn fossil fuels for power, requiring gas turbines, huge tanks of diesel fuel kept on-site in case of a power outage or good old-fashioned coal. This has devastating environmental and health consequences, both immediately for local communities and in the long term for the entire world. 

Communities that neighbor data centers have reported brown or unsafe drinking water, unending noise, and in one lawsuit against Elon Musk’s xAI centers in Memphis, extreme health risks; Memphis residents “are feeling it in their lungs because of the fossil fuels that are being burned,” Marx said.

Tennessee state representative Justin Pearson speaks at a rally in opposition to Elon Musk’s data center in Memphis on April 25, 2025.

Brandon Dill for The Washington Post via Getty Images

And as decades of climate research prove, burning additional fossil fuels is only going to exacerbate the effects of climate change. That’ll lead to even more extreme weather, health risks and natural disasters. As Marx put it in his book, “The world will suffer through the worsening natural disasters fueled by the quest for computation by some of the most powerful people on the planet.”

With data centers and their fossil fuels, we’re fundamentally reshaping the planet for AI. So anti-data center movements are asking: Is it worth it?

“How much computation do we really need here?” Marx asked in our conversation. “How many resources are we willing to dedicate to this vision of the future? And is this technology really delivering in such a way that expending all those resources is justified?”

The answer — for many data center neighbors in Memphis, Oregon, Chile, Ireland and thousands of other communities across the globe — is an unflinching no.

title: Yelp’s AI Assistant Can Call a Restaurant and Join the Waitlist for You
snippet: The updated agent also can tell you if it’s going to rain and maybe you shouldn’t book that outdoor table.
fullText:
Hate calling restaurants to check wait times? Yelp is rolling out a new AI-powered tool to handle just that, along with other tools as the platform deepens its employment of agentic artificial intelligence.

“This release is another step forward as we transform Yelp with AI, with updates across every category on Yelp, from booking a table at a restaurant to hiring a pro for a home project,” Akhil Kuduvalli Ramesh, Yelp’s chief product officer, said in a statement. 

Yelp expands its AI offerings

Just months after launching an updated AI assistant, Yelp Assistant, that can book reservations for you, Yelp is expanding its AI integrations with a new AI agent. Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes. As personal and shopping assistants become more widely used, new reports show the hardships faced by both businesses and customers: Businesses must contend with an influx of calls and emails from bots, while human customers must compete with AI agents to make reservations.    

			

More from CNET

Yelp Assistant now works with OpenTable, allowing you access to thousands of restaurants across the US. You can simply ask the assistant for recommendations on “dog-friendly coffee shops” and booking help.

You can also use Yelp Waitlist to get in line before you arrive. After you join the line, Yelp Assistant will send you status updates, such as when your table becomes available. 

Check for Me will call restaurants on your behalf to check wait times in real time and text you with updates within a few minutes.Yelp

Yelp Assistant gets personal

Yelp is further expanding its Assistant capabilities while also adding more personalization. 

A new feature, Keep Me Posted, lets you tailor your reminders based on your personal schedule. With the feature, you can have Yelp Assistant send you weekend date night ideas every Thursday or dog-friendly hikes once a month. These personal AI agents that execute tasks on your behalf are becoming increasingly popular. Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots recently hit the market, and Google is continuously incorporating agentic AI into its booking and planning services. 

Yelp Assistant’s personalization will also apply to conversations by referencing past chats and your Yelp review history. For instance, if you’ve recently chatted on Yelp for vegan restaurants near you, the Assistant will ask if you’re interested in more vegan options. 

For further personalization, the app can now reference local weather forecasts when you make reservations, so you don’t book an outdoor patio on a night it’s supposed to pour. And a new feature, My Lists, lets you save, rank and promote your favorite local businesses, and then Yelp will give you more tailored recommendations based on your lists. 

Yelp initially debuted its AI Assistant in 2024, but these new integrations and features show how Yelp is evolving as AI tools become more adept at actually doing things, not just telling you things.

title: Mamdani says feds have abdicated on AI, urges New Yorkers to push back
snippet: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Monday night that New Yorkers must resist the narrative that an AI takeover is inevitable and demand regulations that protect the public and put power back in their hands.
fullText:
Two of New York’s sweethearts, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist and “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, spoke about AI at Webster Hall in Manhattan on Monday night, with Glazer posing questions to the mayor about the future of AI in society.  

Mamdani encouraged New Yorkers to resist the overwhelming feeling that AI is inevitably coming for their jobs, their kids’ minds, and their dignity, and to take back control instead. 

His message came at a moment when the federal government is doing little to regulate AI, leaving cities to act on their own. At The People’s AI Assembly, an event hosted by the AI Now Institute, a think tank that explores the social implications of AI, Mamdani argued that the technology’s rapid rollout is not inevitable and that public officials should hold AI companies accountable.

Last month, Mamdani ordered a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools. Glazer, a parent, said the technology’s arrival in classrooms unsettles her.

“It just makes me nervous. It feels so non-consensual, as though…this has to be in schools. It wasn’t two years ago. Why does it have to be in schools?” she said.

Over the summer, the mayor also introduced a policy that would require landlords, brokers, and real estate platforms to clearly disclose when a property’s listing photos or videos are made with AI. The policy is aimed at protecting New Yorkers from getting “house-phished,” or tricked by misleading listings.

Both moves challenge the assumption that schools and the public must simply accept AI as it arrives.

“Nothing has to be,” Mamdani said at the event Monday. “There’s a creep that comes with this, and there’s an intent to overwhelm that leaves people feeling as if there is simply no option.”

He said there has been a “reckless adoption of technology without any kind of a reckoning with the limitations of that technology,” citing the U.S. military’s February strike on a school in Iran that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children. Officials involved in the Pentagon’s internal investigation have told Bloomberg that overreliance on AI in targeting was one factor in the attack.

“There is this desire to speak about [AI] as if it is infallible, as if it cannot be questioned, as if the only people who can regulate it are the ones who are currently developing it,” Mamdani said, noting that Facebook made similar arguments back in 2008. “What it really is,’ he continued, “is an attempt to escape any kind of accountability at any level, without also jeopardizing the potential valuation from an IPO.”

Anthropic is expected to debut on the public markets this year, and OpenAI has said it will go public in 2027. 

Mamdani criticized the “complete abdication of federal law” when it comes to AI. 

“At a national level, when the conversation is about artificial intelligence, it’s so often framed in this language of an arms race with China, and any of the humanistic concern, we just push to the side in a language of national competition,” the mayor said. 

President Donald Trump’s Superintelligence Task Force, announced earlier this month, largely focuses on allowing powerful AI companies to self-regulate, rather than creating new federal restrictions. That comes despite growing fears about AI’s effect on every facet of human life, including warnings from whistleblowers at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI that AI could lead to human extinction. 

“As we are looking at what comes after this federal administration, there has to be a very different kind of framework in how we think about AI, talk about AI, the accountability we’re willing to bring forward when it comes to that,” Mamdani said.

title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
snippet: Microsoft wants enterprises to closely watch the agents that employees use with systems not controlled by AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.
fullText:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes as Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog, Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward. 

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”

On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too. 

Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies. The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents, which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.

title: Replika’s founder built the AI assistant she pitched at Disrupt 12 years ago
snippet: Eugenia Kuyda's newest startup Wabi is positioned to take advantage of an idea she had more than a decade ago. Wabi offers a personal AI assistant with a twist, free and downloadable to anyone today.
fullText:
Twelve years ago today, Eugenia Kuyda stood up onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt and presented a conversational chatbot called IO that acted as a lifestyle concierge to help people book restaurants and vacations along with other tasks. 

IO, the first product from her startup Luka, came before the deep learning breakthroughs that would eventually lead to today’s large language models. “It still worked,” Kuyda told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It was pretty magical … but, of course, it’s nowhere near what we have today.”

Luka ended up becoming Replika, the popular AI chatbot companion company. Last year, Kuyda left as CEO of Replika and founded Wabi. 

The technology has finally caught up with her original vision for Luka, just in time for Wabi to take on a wave of new personal AI assistants such as Muse and Instinct, which promise to do everything from manage your inbox to find you the best flight deals. 

On Monday, Kuyda officially launched Wabi for all users, a multiplayer personal AI assistant that functions as a messenger app, allowing users to maintain multiple agentic threads dedicated to different tasks and long-term goals. Within each thread, users can build and use custom apps, like a weight-loss tracker inside a health thread or an app showing nearby children’s events inside a family thread. 

The launch is something of a pivot for Wabi, though Kuyda describes it as more of an evolution. When TechCrunch covered Wabi’s initial launch last year, along with its $20 million pre-seed round, it was described as more of a social platform where you could create mini apps with prompts that you could share with friends or across the app. 

Over the past year, Kuyda said the team realized that while people love personal software rather than “one size fits all solutions in the App Store,” they “maybe don’t want to spend a lot of time, or any time, building it.” 

With Wabi 2.0, the agent decides what apps to build. The moment you connect it to your email, it automatically spins up a number of threads and apps to start with, and users can add to that by requesting custom apps or starting new threads. 

“It’s doing what Instinct and Muse do, but it also has all these apps, which helps users do more stuff,” Kuyda said.

App-building isn’t Wabi’s only differentiator. Kuyda is also betting on its multithreaded, multiplayer design.

“It’s not just everything in one single thread like with Instinct and Muse, where you get buried in the information that it sends you every day,” Kuyda said. “Single thread experiences, if you think about it, get worse over time because it’s just so much context in one endless conversation.”

The longer an AI chatbot conversation goes on, the more likely it is to hallucinate, lose track of context, or respond in ways that would otherwise be blocked by safety guardrails, according to interviews with AI researchers.

Image Credits:Wabi

Threads can also be shared, functioning as group chats. 

“Today, all the agentic apps are just [conversations] between you and the agent, and I feel like it should be a lot more about bringing people together in a group chat together,” Kuyda said. “Not you doing it separately with your AI, and I’m doing it separately with my AI … I don’t think anyone has yet cracked multiplayer.” 

Kuyda walked TechCrunch through some of her own shared threads. In one with her boyfriend, a row of apps along the top helps the two of them connect and find things to do together, including a live music tracker, an app that asks a question every day about their relationship, a running list of restaurant suggestions, important events from their shared calendar, and a list of books they’re reading together with suggestions for what to read next. 

In her more family-focused thread, there is an app tracking her daughter’s schedule, another for finding kid-friendly events nearby, and another that quizzes her daughter on Japanese. 

Within any shared chat, users can share as much or as little as they want, from email and calendar information to bank account details.

“So my partner can ask Wabi in the chat, ‘Is Eugenia free next Thursday?’ or ‘Did she buy those tickets?’” Kuyda said. She noted that access is scoped to individual chats, and everyone in a chat can see when someone’s personal information is requested.

On privacy more broadly, Wabi is SOC 2 compliant, meaning its data security controls have been independently audited. Wabi runs entirely in the cloud, and most user data is stored in the U.S., Kuyda said. 

“My previous company Replika worked on AI that will make people feel … less lonely,” Kuyda said. “To a degree, that is [in Wabi] as well. AI can bring people together, even when it comes to just helping you spend time better together in real life, whether it’s going out and seeing a concert together or finding the next book that you will read together.”

Wabi is free for now, and the company hasn’t settled on a business model yet. Kuyda said Wabi is in talks to raise more funds.

title: Amazon launches two Bee AI recorders to remember everything you say
snippet: Just over a year after acquiring the AI company, Bee, Amazon has officially unveiled two of its first AI wearables, so you never forget what was said. more…
fullText:
Just over a year after acquiring the AI company, Bee, Amazon has officially unveiled two of its first AI wearables, so you never forget what was said.

Amazon announced two models: the Bee Frontier and the Bee Eclipse. Both can be considered wearables, with one taking on a bracelet form factor that works just fine clipped to a shirt. The Eclipse is a magnetic version of the always-listening device for use with Qi2 or MagSafe-equipped phones.

The Frontier is not dissimilar to the first preview Bee introduced before it was purchased by Amazon. At the time, the company had seemingly high hopes for being a genuine cornerstone of people’s lives to make their lives easier.

Amazon says both models are designed with “privacy principles” in mind, noting that a visible LED indicates when the Bee Frontier or Eclipse is listening. That’s what they do, after all. Both are designed to stay active and compile your ideas, thoughts, and even nonsense into reminders or notes, based on what Bee’s AI model decides you might need.

	

All of that can be found in the companion app, whether on mobile or desktop. Users can connect their Google Account to let it access emails and calendar information. That feeds into the selling idea that Bee becomes your personal assistant so you don’t miss out on a thing.

As for hardware, the Bee Frontier wearable is IP67 and rated for seven days of battery. The magnetic Eclipse model is able to power through a longer workload with up to 21 days of battery on a charge.

Of course, Amazon also added Alexa+ and Amazon.com integration into how the Bee wearables operate. The devices will be able to surface products based on your anticipated needs. That’s fun.

The Bee Frontier is available now for $74.99, while the Bee Eclipse will goi on sale “soon” starting at $99.99.

title: Apple is right about the wild west of AI, and the growing backlash
snippet: Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak didn’t hold back when he described the most ambitious figures in the AI race as the “lunatic fringe” of Silicon Valley. The piece suggested that the iPhone maker is hoping to position itself as being on the right side of a growing AI backlash. Given the pace of development, trying to predict the future of AI is a risky business, but I do think Apple is absolutely right about the dangers … more…
fullText:
Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak didn’t hold back when he described the most ambitious figures in the AI race as the “lunatic fringe” of Silicon Valley. The piece suggested that the iPhone maker is hoping to position itself as being on the right side of a growing AI backlash.

Given the pace of development, trying to predict the future of AI is a risky business, but I do think Apple is absolutely right about the dangers …

The piece cites the familiar refrain that Apple’s slow pace when it comes to AI features could see the company being left behind.

Virtually [all other tech giants] have flung themselves into the AI arms race, pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into training ever more intelligent thinking machines. While Apple trains its own models, it is nowhere near the technology’s frontier, leaving the company vulnerable to being left behind if super-smart AI transforms industry and society in the coming years.

Joswiak counters that the company is focused on launching AI features that will perform useful tasks for ordinary people, and that Apple’s privacy focus will become increasingly valuable in the context of an AI backlash against a “lunatic fringe” of unconstrained acceleration of a technology we can barely control today.

Lunacy is certainly a good word to describe a world in which AI companies fear that their work may destroy humanity, but they are even more afraid that one of their competitors will beat them to it.

AI is the first technological development that has ever threatened such a wide variety of jobs, with a huge number of positions likely to be eliminated in fields as diverse as truck driving, marketing, and software development. Academics have even expressed concern that future generations will no longer become mathematicians or scientific researchers over fears that those roles will be made redundant by AI.

For example, math professor Giordano Scarciotti recently said that when AI models are solving in days problems academics have worked on for years, the results could be devastating because it will seem pointless to future generations to even attempt this type of work.

I explore a potentially devastating consequence of AI’s growing capabilities: what happens when the next generation of talented students no longer sees a reason to become mathematicians? The implications could extend far beyond mathematics and affect the future of scientific progress itself.

	

He argues that when today’s students see no future in academic research, this may leave AI models technically solving scientific problems, but with no one left to understand the implications and to apply the findings in meaningful ways. Similar effects are likely to occur in software development, where there are fewer and fewer humans able to understand the code being generated by increasingly advanced AI models.

The nightmare scenario here is that AI takes on ever more tasks as once-expert human beings become sidelined and marginalized because there’s no point in future generations attempting to compete. And if you think that’s baseless paranoia, I highly recommend listening to the podcast series Suspicious Minds: AI and the Apocalypse.

Quite how much power Apple has to fight back against such a dystopian future is questionable, but it could certainly be argued that at least the company is not applying its vast resources to accelerating the effect. Here’s hoping that the AI backlash grows sufficiently rapidly and loudly that politicians are forced to take steps to bring the current wild west of AI under some form of control.

title: Apple Intelligence reportedly coming to China in December, but without Siri AI
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple plans to finally launch Apple Intelligence in China in December, although some important features could still be missing. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple plans to finally launch Apple Intelligence in China in December, although some important features could still be missing. Here are the details.

Apple Intelligence to see limited launch in China with iOS 27.3

Earlier today, a report from the South China Morning Post claimed that Chinese regulators had approved the use of Alibaba’s AI models to power Apple Intelligence, following preliminary approval for the platform’s rollout in July.

The report noted that the timing of the approval was particularly relevant, as the iPhone Duo is scheduled to launch in China next week.

Now, Bloomberg reports that Apple “is planning to launch Apple Intelligence in the region in December as part of an upcoming iOS 27.3 update,” although the launch “will exclude the new Siri AI assistant and other features announced this year,” according to the publication’s sources.

The move comes after a lengthy and complicated effort to bring Apple Intelligence to China, where local regulations governing AI-generated content, security assessments, and algorithm registration have forced Apple to take a different approach than in other markets.

Here’s Bloomberg:

In order to get Apple Intelligence approved, the company had to make some concessions. Unlike in other countries, the platform has guardrails developed with China’s Alibaba Group Holding Ltd., including a filter that allows the government to approve ongoing updates to the AI models. Apple is also working with Baidu Inc. on features related to search and Siri.

On Sept. 29, Apple received Chinese permits allowing recent iPhones to support the use of Apple Intelligence and Alibaba AI models, including Tongyi Wanxiang and Qwen.

The report notes that Apple Intelligence’s launch in China will not feature “the company’s in-house image-generation tools,” while certain “features for generating text will also be limited in some applications.”

According to Bloomberg, the initial rollout will include Genmoji for creating custom emoji, Apple’s AI-powered notification summaries, writing tools, and the Clean Up feature in Photos, which lets users remove unwanted objects from images.

The report notes that it is unclear whether these features will be enough to win over Chinese consumers, as local smartphone makers have already introduced their own AI capabilities:

With AI services proliferating on rival phones from Huawei Technologies Co., Xiaomi Corp., Oppo Guangdong Mobile Telecommunications Corp., Vivo Mobile Communication Co. and others in China, it’s unclear how much Apple will benefit from launching a two-year-old set of relatively basic AI features in the country.

Interestingly, today’s report came just one day after Apple said in the footnotes of its HomeView announcement that it is “working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward” to launch Siri AI in Europe, where the assistant also remains unavailable due to regulatory issues.

title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems
snippet: The US has ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and third-party services built using its technology, citing national security concerns.
fullText:
The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.

The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said.

The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models.

China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.  

The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.

Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week.

The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares.

The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report.

In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude.

title: Gemini app rolling out Gemini 4 Argon to AI Pro and AI Ultra
snippet: Following the announcement at the end of September, Gemini 4 Argon is starting to roll out to the Gemini app, Google Antigravity, and more. more…
fullText:
Following the announcement at the end of September, Gemini 4 Argon is starting to roll out to the Gemini app, Google Antigravity, and more.

Gemini app 

In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Argon is available for both Google AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Last month, initial availability was just for the Ultra ($99.99+) tier. 

Google says to expect “frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows” in the app. Additionally:

“Argon answers questions more directly with less hedging, doesn’t repeat itself more than necessary, and skips clichés throughout the responses.” Additionally, it “follows style instructions more reliably than any of our previous Gemini models.”

“For longer tasks, it keeps you in the loop by sharing its progress more often and more effectively.”

Given the “major improvements” in coding performance, Google is letting users “switch between chatting and coding” within the Gemini app for macOS. Users will specifically have direct access to Antigravity’s agentic coding interface in the consumer client for building apps, web experiences, and more.

	

Meanwhile, there will be a new toggle in the main chat window that lets you switch from chat to tasks (previously Spark). As of today, AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers will see 3.5 Flash-Lite, 3.8 Flash, 3.1 Pro, and 4 Argon in the model picker.

AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers can also access Gemini 4 Argon in AI Mode.

Google Antigravity + more

	

In the Antigravity desktop app and Antigravity CLI, the new model requires AI Ultra. Google today shared more examples of how it has been using Argon with its internal version of Antigravity across Chrome, Gemma, YouTube, and more:

“Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase. Piping multiple clean code changes at a time, Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome’s billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes.”

“Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the upstream pull requests (optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes.”

“Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms.”

AI Ultra is also required for Argon access in AI Studio and Android Studio (Canary).

Argon is available in the Gemini API at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30, 2026. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

On the science front, Google is offering 10,000 scientists the “highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free of charge for 6 months.” Applications are now open.

title: Meta says it has fixed an issue that let its Ray-Ban smart glasses record on their own
snippet: As privacy complaints continue to dominate the conversation around Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, the company is now fixing an issue that was letting the glasses record on their own without the user prompting the recording. more…
fullText:
As privacy complaints continue to dominate the conversation around Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, the company is now fixing an issue that was letting the glasses record on their own without the user prompting the recording.

A number of Ray-Ban Meta users on Reddit note that, recently, their glasses have been invoking Meta AI and, in turn, voice recording, without prompts. The “Hey Meta” wake word was not used and, for some, not even enabled. One user says this happened across three separate pairs of glasses. 

The glasses still alert users to the recordings by lighting up the LED on the inner frame of the glasses, but it’s obviously a bit concerning to randomly have the glasses start recording on their own, even if it is audio only. 

Speaking to Android Authority, Meta confirmed that the issue has been “resolved.”

	

This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.

The cause isn’t mentioned, but it comes at a time where Meta’s smart glasses are under continual scrutiny for privacy. Meta, in trying to correct its course, has made adjustments to its glasses including rolling out a mandatory update that disables the camera on its glasses if someone tampers with the LED privacy light.

title: SpaceX alum’s aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation
snippet: Reliable Robotics extended its Series D round with $115 million in equity and $25 million in debt.
fullText:
Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.

The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date. 

“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.

And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.

Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.

Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.

The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station. 

Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.

“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.

The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)

While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.

“It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.”
