title: Otter.ai raises $320 million from General Catalyst’s growth fund for its meeting tool
snippet: Meeting note-taking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend. Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation. […]
fullText:
Meeting note-taking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend. 

Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation.

The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data. 

Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The company said it’s now approaching new milestones, but didn’t provide updated figures.

The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting note-taking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn.

“Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it – a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, Partner and Co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.”

There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola, and Read AI; new entrants like Calendly, Wispr, and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill. 

Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced a meeting assistant, a search function that works across apps, and integration with other AI tools. 

Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings. 

“When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or, from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said.

The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send a pre-brief to users with details and background information, with context from previous conversations across surfaces. Plus, it is also trying out a Live Assist feature to let users ask questions to the AI assistant during the meeting to get knowledge.

title: Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving
snippet: Eka Robotics may be the first robotic arm that is actually good at picking a wide range of objects up, and it is so smooth and human-like, it is wowing the industry.
fullText:
Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models. 

That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime.

“They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raguram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch.

In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders. 

Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.”

Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to ten years ago. Take a look for yourself:

Loading the player…

 

What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?”

When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch.

How not to squish the raspberry

These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks, say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point.

“Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.”

Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes.

“Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.”

Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California, Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gigworkers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past that has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them. 

“What EKA is bridging is the generality-performance gap, which plagues a lot of modern robotics,” Agrawal argues.

Making a general-purpose robot useful

Right now, the most generalizable physical AI models—the ones that can attempt lots of different tasks—aren’t particularly good at them. But AI models trained to be highly capable at a single task may not close the business case for a company: The promise of generative AI is that robots can quickly learn multiple tasks, even novel ones.

The current approaches are good at producing robots that are more generally intelligent than before — Astra, ChatGPT’s latest LLM, can operate a robot in an unfamiliar setting and perform tasks with it, but slowly and at a high cost. The promise of a model like Eka’s is that it handles the physicality while a more general model makes decisions about how to solve a problem. Astra, for example, might know that plates get stacked in a cupboard when they come out of the dishwasher, but Eka’s model is capable of picking up a dish without breaking it.

“Most of the field has been focusing on the planning,” Eka co-founder Haarnoja says, “so they approach from the top: high-level intelligence, pushing that down towards the physical. Whereas we think about it from the bottom up.”

Eka still needs to prove itself in the field, though. The company is working in secretive pilots with a number of industrial customers doing pick-and-place and wire manipulation, but the leap from lab to line is almost as big as the gap between sim and real.

“What’s going to be a big challenge is when they work with integrators on real assembly lines, and it needs to run without breaking for an entire year,” Hauser said. The other open question is “‘how generalizable these techniques can be to different tasks?’ What I’ve seen is pick and place, but many industry tasks that are value added involve more than just pick-and-place.”

Agrawal is also focused on deployability; right now, he says Eka’s gripper hardware — which costs less than $1,000 — is rated for 5 million duty cycles, but the ultimate goal is to hit the 20 million cycle bar set by standard industrial arms.

“What we are building is that engineering of how to design entire workflows, but we are starting off being very pragmatic, and saying here are two verticals in pick, arrange, place, and wire handling, let’s make them be home runs,” Agrawal said. “Once we have made home runs on them, the sky is the limit in how much we can do with the approach we are developing.”

Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models.

That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. title: Embedded AI evaluators won’t be an easy solution, Hugging Face’s policy chief says
snippet: The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly "neutral" third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology.
fullText:
AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another.  

However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future.

With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released?

“Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part [of that] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added.

Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the stickier aspects of benchmarking — and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry.

Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations.

“They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said. 

“They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.”

The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face was famously the target of one of those incidents.

Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s decision to hire Accenture as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some critics mocking the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand.

Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily outperform a frontier model, Solaiman shared.

“Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added.

In other words, the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary.

title: AI assistant startup Town nabs unicorn valuation 4 months after launch
snippet: AI assistant startup Town nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures.
fullText:
Town, a two-year-old, San Francisco-based startup developing AI assistants, nabbed a unicorn valuation on Monday, announcing a $108 million Series B funding round co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures. The company launched publicly just four months ago and said it reached millions of dollars in annual recurring revenue in a matter of weeks. It has raised at least $160 million to date, having previously announced a $55 million Series A round in June.

Town — founded by former Plaid CTO Jean-Denis Greze — is one of many AI assistants flooding the market right now. Town targets businesses, giving each employee an AI assistant called a Townie that helps with tasks by connecting to tools such as emails and calendars, as well as other core work systems. Employees’ Townies can talk to each other and share approved information; they can also now work with customers and others outside the company. 

Alongside the funding, Town announced a shared workflow that automatically updates employees’ Townies with new business information rather than requiring each worker to update their own Townie. Andreessen Horowitz, Serena Ventures, and First Round Capital also participated in the round. 

We’ve reached out to the company for comment.

title: Galaxy S26 Ultra is one of the ‘best inventions of 2026’ thanks to its Privacy Display
snippet: A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display. more…
fullText:
A new 2026 roundup has the Galaxy S26 Ultra included in a list of best inventions for the year, all thanks to what it doesn’t display.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra split in a slightly different direction. Instead of a display panel treatment with an anti-gflare coating, Samsung decided to pack an entirely different feature into the panel itself.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display allows users to block certain aspects of the screen from nearby onlookers, effectively circumventing the privacy screen protector so many users opt for.

According to Time‘s “best inventions of 2026” collection, the Galaxy S26 Ultra gets its plaudits for not the phone’s performance necessarily, but the Privacy Display. The listing quotes Samsung’s SVP of Mobile Product Management, who points to its flexible nature.

	

It’s undoubtedly a cool piece of display tech. The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display not only blocks side-angle viewing, but it can do so in isolated portions of the screen to block PIN codes or notifications that drop from the top shade in Android.

It has some drawbacks, though, as we’ve pointed out before. It can be a little inconsistent in certain lighting conditions, and sometimes screen elements can look off. But it’s cool, and a nice addition to a phone that sits at a price range we now consider more affordable than what we’re probably getting here soon.

Time‘s piece goes on to list a couple of other familiar devices, like a lengthy segment on the iPhone Duo, propping it up rather highly. Another product we’re happy to see is the Clicks Power Keyboard.

AS for whether the Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra will get a Privacy Display, rumors suggest it could happen. Time will tell as Samsung plans to launch the devices early next year.

title: Apple strikes deal with AI startup that lets musicians rework recorded music
snippet: The EU’s List of Acquisitions website was updated today with details of a deal struck in June between Apple and Samplab, a Swiss startup that described itself as offering “music production for the age of AI.” Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The EU’s List of Acquisitions website was updated today with details of a deal struck in June between Apple and Samplab, a Swiss startup that described itself as offering “music production for the age of AI.” Here are the details.

Apple’s string of AI deals continues

Last week, the List of Acquisitions section of the EU’s DMA website was updated with details on Apple’s move to acqui-hire Huxe, a startup founded by former NotebookLM engineers that specialized in generating personalized audio briefings and podcast-style content using AI.

Today, the list was updated yet again, revealing another deal involving Apple and an AI audio company.

Apple Inc. (“Apple”), through a subsidiary, will acquire certain assets of Samplab GmbH (“Samplab”) and offer employment to and hire certain Samplab employees. Samplab develops audio editing tools. Apple (together with its group companies) designs, manufactures and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and sells a variety of related services.

Following the deal, Samplab’s website now redirects to Apple’s, while its social media accounts and YouTube channel appear to have been scrubbed of their previous posts and videos.

Previously, Samplab’s website described its “ultimate audio editor for musicians” as a tool that allowed creators to “edit audio files as if you were working with MIDI.” It also touted its ability to:

Detect and edit chords

They stay in key when you change them.

You can even export them as a midi file.

Make any samples sound good together

Samplab matches their tempo and key.

Easily adapt chords, melodies and drums.

Granular stem separation

Separate stems in any audio and

freely modify individual notes.

While Apple has not commented on the acquisition, it isn’t hard to imagine Samplab’s technology eventually making its way into Logic Pro or GarageBand, or even enhancing the audio editing capabilities of Final Cut Pro.

title: YouTube Music rolling out AI labels in the Now Playing screen
snippet: In response to more AI-generated content appearing on streaming services, YouTube Music is adding a new AI label directly to the player. more…
fullText:
In response to more AI-generated content appearing on streaming services, YouTube Music is adding a new AI label directly to the player.

When a song is “created primarily using generative AI,” you’ll soon see a label on the Now Playing screen. This includes “using a generative model to create the composition and vocals.” The goal is to “make it as easy as possible for viewers and listeners to have the right information and clarity when it comes to the music they listen to.”

It appears just below the song name next to the artist/channel. This “AI” badge with an info icon opens a “How this was made” bottom sheet. 

YouTube Music explains how this was “Made with AI: This audio was altered or fully generated using AI” with a link to learn more. 

	

YouTube is using its own detection tools and “teaming up with music partners” to identify AI-generated tracks. 

The rollout starts today. In the future, these AI labels for music will come to the main YouTube app.

title: I Tried Amazing Security Tech for Renters From a Company You’ve Never Heard Of
snippet: It’s the year of window cams, and Baseus has my favorite model yet. Here’s why renters and second-story homes should consider it.
fullText:
Tyler Lacoma/CNET		

	

		

									

						Baseus PimeSentinel W1 Window Camera					

					

	8.5

	
					

			

	

		

			

				Pros & Cons			

			

			

							

					
						4K resolution					
				

							

					
						Great magnetic, indoor design					
				

							

					
						Adjustable camera angle (unusual in window cams)					
				

							

					
						MicroSD card slot for free local storage					
				

							

					
						Free motion and AI object detection for people, vehicles and animals					
				

							

					
						Privacy and motion zone options to customize where and how the camera monitors					
				

							

					
						Simple, effective app					
				

					

			

							

					
						Overly sensitive motion and object detection can trigger false alerts from shadows, though privacy and motion zones help					
				

							

					
						Night vision is only passable, and requires a least a little light to work well					
				

					

	

		

It’s tough to find good security devices for renters because of the restrictions on what changes they can make to their homes and all the fine print in their leases. Window cameras are a happy exception — adhesive-mounted cams that stick to windows and allow you to monitor carports, parking spaces, yards, visitors and more. If you don’t have room for a traditional security camera, it’s a versatile — and affordable — alternative.

My new favorite dedicated window cam comes from Baseus, a company that has stood out in this growing category in 2026. If you haven’t heard of it, you’ll want to keep it in mind. Like Anker, with its many tech lines, including Eufy security, Baseus is a Chinese company that makes a bit of everything, including solid-performing security products at reasonable prices.

The Baseus PrimeSentinel W1 Window Camera ($100) offers a particularly clever design and no-subscription management, although you may need to do a little work in settings to customize everything to your liking. If you’ve dealt with other vehicles taking your spot, people vandalizing your car, strangers on your steps, package theft or similar problems, consider using a camera like this on a window near your door. Here’s how it works.

			

More from CNET

Design and a very easy installation

I was originally very skeptical about using a security camera to look through a window, since glare is a constant problem, the right angle is hard to find and the camera can get in the way of shades or curtains. The first cam to change my mind was Wyze’s version, launched earlier this year. Baseus, however, has a model with a design I like much better, albeit at a higher price.

Instead of using Velcro like the Wyze model, the Baseus cam has a magnetic frame. Stick it to a clean window and the small Baseus cam locks on automatically. All you need is an outlet somewhere near the window to plug the camera in.

The Baseus magnetic frame is a step above other versions I’ve tested.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

But that’s not the only thing I like about its design. You can also manually angle the orb-like camera lense, shifting it downward to focus on things below the window. That’s a helpful feature if you live a story or two up in an apartment building and need to angle the camera down to watch your car parked directly below or a similar area.

A side slot makes room for a microSD card, which allows you to store video locally without paying any subscription fees or risking privacy issues with cloud video storage. I suggest grabbing a microSD card along with this cam if you choose to buy.

Video performance and capabilities

The Baseus cam has a 4K resolution, unusual at this price.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Another useful feature of the Baseus window cam is its 4K resolution, which can be tough to find in cameras under $100. It provides extra detail and worked quite well in my testing. The 130-degree field of view captured a good swath of my yard and should be sufficient for most viewing needs.

The magnetic lock design holds the camera directly against the window, minimizing glare, although some slight distortion may occur when the sun shines directly on the lens. A unique feature lets you flip the video 180 degrees, which can be helpful when positioning the camera based on your windows, the location of the nearest outlet and how unobtrusive you want the cam to be.

Baseus’s app and live view offer plenty of detail.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Video recording and histories also worked well, although snapshots were significantly more blurry than the 4K live view. The camera comes with low-light night vision, which is fine. It’s not going to compete with the more advanced night vision you’ll find on modern cameras, but as long as there’s a little nearby light, I was able to pick out the details. If your area goes completely dark at night, it may be hard for the camera to capture much.

The camera also includes a mic and speaker for two-way audio. It’s funny seeing this feature on a window camera, because while I know it’s common, audio is mostly useless here. You won’t be able to hear much of anything outside, and shouting through the speaker won’t reach outdoors either. At most, you may be able to alert someone inside the house if, for example, you’re at work and see someone smashing car windows in the parking lot.

App controls, settings and smart features

Baseus has a simple and intuitive app.Screenshot by Tyler Lacoma/CNET

The Baseus app is relatively simple, with sections for viewing event history, changing settings, watching the live feed and more. There are no surprises, but it’s worth diving into the settings to improve the camera’s accuracy.

Baseus doesn’t do subscriptions, but you do get detection features for free. That includes not only basic motion detection, but also options to enable person, pet and vehicle detection, along with sensitivity controls.

While glare isn’t a problem when viewing videos, there seems to be just enough reflection for the camera to mistake people or shadows moving around the room for a “person spotted” outside when the light is right. The camera occasionally appeared to be triggered by moving trees as well and was too sensitive overall, even when I lowered it to the lowest sensitivity setting.

Privacy zones are important for the neighbors.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

To avoid mistakes and frequent triggers, I turned to another feature in the app: Baseus includes the ability to add both privacy zones and motion zones. Privacy zones place black sections on the camera’s recording so they don’t show up in videos, which is useful for blocking a neighbor’s yard or parking spot and avoiding issues with privacy.

Motion zones and object settings take a little work to get right.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

However, the privacy zone feature didn’t always block object detection in that area, so I also used motion detection zones to control which spots the camera watched. Between the privacy and motion zones, I was able to wrangle the camera into sending reasonable alerts about the activity I cared about.

I also suggest leaving pet detection off, since it offers the least security value. Hopefully, Baseus will release updates to reduce false alerts overall. In the meantime, you can turn off object and motion detection entirely, or enable privacy mode to temporarily disable the camera.

What about Baseus? Is this brand safe to use?

Before recommending a relatively little-known Chinese security brand, I researched its track record, looking for significant data breaches, privacy concerns or other red flags. Baseus, much like Anker, doesn’t have any obvious security issues. You can view the Baseus privacy policy here, which goes over the information it collects and notes that privacy laws in other countries (and certain states, such as California) do apply to the data it handles. It’s a little rough, but does include plenty of useful information.

I found no notable security incidents involving Baseus. However, the company says authorized employees may access encrypted personal information. It also says it doesn’t collect financial information, relying instead on third-party services to secure that data. But as I previously mentioned, you can use a microSD card for local storage, so you won’t be storing video directly on Baseus servers.

Overall, I’d like to know a bit more about the company’s security practices, relationship with the government and data storage, but there’s nothing right now that would make me hesitant to suggest the company to users.

Final thoughts on the Baseus PrimeSentinel W1 Window Camera

This cam is a particularly good option for monitoring through a window if you can’t install an outdoor camera.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

With its 4K resolution, magnetic design, rotatable lens and free local video storage, the Baseus W1 is my favorite window camera so far—a strong showing from a relatively unknown name in home security. At $100, it costs more than some window cameras, but its features make it a good value. I’ll be testing other options this year, including a new window camera from Eufy, but for now, the W1 is my top choice.

I’d like to see some improvements with its object detection and recognition, which triggered too frequently and seemed occasionally affected by reflections, although I managed to improve results by using the welcome privacy and motion zone settings. Otherwise, this is an excellent choice for renters who may want to watch their cars but can’t use an outdoor cam, and anyone else who has a spot on their window to keep an eye on things.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: Gemini 4 Argon is now rolling out to Google’s Antigravity for AI Pro subscribers
snippet: Google is now rolling out support for Gemini 4 Argon to Antigravity, its AI coding tool. more…
fullText:
Google is now rolling out support for Gemini 4 Argon to Antigravity, its AI coding tool.

Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s latest flagship AI model, announced at the end of September and having widely rolled out to users earlier this week. Now, it’s also available within Antigravity.

Antigravity is an agentic development platform, as Google describes it, which leverages AI and agents to assist in coding and building apps. Google announced that Argon would be available in Antigravity earlier this week, and it’s now actively rolling out to AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers – we’re seeing it live on our end, too.

Google restricts every free AI Pro trial from Pixel & more compared to paid subscribers

In a post on Twitter/X, Google adds that there’s “a separate weekly-only Argon quota” on top of the existing quota for Gemini 3.8 Flash, meaning you’ll be able to use the model that best suits your needs. Google says that Argon is “designed to tackle your hardest problems.”

	

Google also provided a host of examples of how Argon in Antigravity has been used internally, including:

YouTube comment optimization: Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms.

Debugging Wing drone physics simulator: Argon in Antigravity reviewed Wing’s proprietary internal drone physics simulator, reasoning through the underlying physics and math rather than just the structure of the code. It highlighted areas for improved physics simulations and proposed 18 targeted modelling improvements across aerodynamics, propulsion, and structural dynamics to resolve long-standing legacy issues.

Burning down the backlog: Argon in Antigravity took an aging queue of 134 open bug reports spanning multiple services, and ran agents to work out which were still real, cross-referencing commit histories, checking whether candidate fixes actually reached production, and inspecting live telemetry for whether the error still occurs. In under 3 hours it closed 97 stale or duplicate bugs with documented commit proof (a 72.4% queue reduction) and sorted the remaining 37 by owner with no unassigned tickets left.

Migrating legacy code: For decades, vital scientific research has been locked inside fragile legacy codebases like Fortran. Using a custom skill within Antigravity, a team deployed Argon to map and execute a complete rewrite into modern Rust. Argon autonomously delivered the modernized codebase, achieving a 1.8x performance boost and memory safety while giving scientists a robust foundation for future work.

Performing security audits: Argon in Antigravity was used to audit a batch of access-control changes. Argon traced how permissions actually flowed at runtime rather than just reading the code diff, and found four critical security bugs. Two earlier frontier models had audited the identical code and both concluded there were zero security holes.

Triaging production support tickets: Argon in Antigravity batch-processes dozens of tickets from an on-call rotation. It sorts them by issue type, tracing root causes through the code and logs, proposing fixes and drafting the replies for human approval. This has freed up 2-3 hours per shift, enabling the team to focus on resolving issues faster.

Marketing website localization: The Antigravity DevRel team used Argon in Antigravity to localize hundreds of pages of developer documentation into 17 languages in a matter of hours. This improved the accessibility and UX of the website by shrinking a multi-week process down to hours and shifting human effort exclusively to high-quality review.

Accelerating data center pipeline modernization: Demonstrating how AI-augmented execution helps teams do more with less, a Data Science Technical Program Manager leveraged Argon in Antigravity to fast-track development of a 3,200-line Google Data Center fleet analytics pipeline (Python, SQL, and dashboards) into production in days. Pairing with Argon to rapidly resolve complex multi-system edge cases, eliminate hardcoded legacy assets, and optimize timeseries queries against timeouts drove end-to-end efficiency — delivering a clean, production-grade, and extensible architecture for fleet-scale analytics.

Vetting sales prospects: Argon in Antigravity built an automated qualification workflow for an account executive in Ads sales that checks prospective company website traffic, confirms the site has clear conversion funnels, and cross-references the sales database to see whether the account is a qualified prospect. This reduced research time by 90%, saving the account executive upwards of 10 hours of manual work each week so they can spend time on direct client outreach instead.

Financial planning and analysis: With custom finance plugins, a finance lead used Argon in Antigravity for end-to-end financial reconciliations, budget tracking, contract extraction, and daily executive briefings across 80 separate workflows. Over seven business days, 15.5 hours of human direction produced about 335 human-equivalent hours of validated financial output, saving more than eight weeks of manual work.

After releasing macOS 27.2 Golden Gate beta 4 last week, Apple is now rolling out the first Release Candidate ahead of the system’s official launch in the coming weeks

macOS 27.2 adds support for five additional languages for Siri AI: French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. The feature launched last month with English-only support, with Apple promising to expand language availability during its Surprise and Shine event.

One particularly frustrating bug reported in beta 4 causes windows in Electron-based apps to randomly stop responding to dragging attempts. Restarting the Mac temporarily resolves the issue, but it can eventually return.

title: Nothing reportedly launching two pairs of smart glasses, one with barely any AI
snippet: A reliable source says that Nothing is building out its own AI smart glasses that feature ChatGPT integration, a camera, and two very different models. more…
fullText:
A reliable source says that Nothing is building out its own AI smart glasses that feature ChatGPT integration, a camera, and two very different models.

WinFuture’s Roland Quandt says on Bluesky that Nothing is preparing to launch two new smart glasses models, and they sound wildly different.

One pair would be similar to the Ray-Ban Meta lineup with a built-in camera and AI features such as translation. While Nothing as an avid Android user might seem like one to hop on the Android XR train, it sounds like that’s probably not the case given Quandt says these are bringing integration with ChatGPT rather than Gemini. That’s not a new pivot on Nothing’s part, though, as the company has been building out ChatGPT integration for a while in its other products.

The other pair of smart glasses, though, would take a much simpler approach.

	

These would work as a pair of headphones with the ability to take calls and interact with your phone’s voice assistant, but they’d lack a camera or any direct AI integrations. Both models are said to offer photochromic lenses, otherwise known as “transition” lenses and commonly found on other smart glasses.

Prior reporting on Nothing’s efforts to build smart glasses pinned a release date sometime in 2027. The dual strategy here is certainly interesting, especially given a recent report that suggested Nothing would go all-in on AI devices going forward.

title: The fossil fuel comeback is here
snippet: The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows. fullText:
The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new report shows.

Electricity demand is also climbing faster than it has in more than a decade with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid. Despite those growing demands, the Trump administration has sought to hobble the wind and solar industries in favor of fossil fuels.

America’s energy landscape is already shifting as a result, according to the report published last week by the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund and research firm Atlas Public Policy. If all the gas projects in the development pipeline complete construction, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades, the authors warn.

“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point”

“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says.

While the US still generates 60 percent of its electricity from fossil fuels, renewables have quickly gained ground. Wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal for the first time in 2024. Solar was the fastest-growing source of new electricity generation that year, accounting for 81 percent of added capacity. Globally, solar has become the cheapest power source in most of the world.

Then Donald Trump stepped into his second term as president with a plan to “drill, baby, drill” for fossil fuels, his preferred power source for energy-hungry data centers. His administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects by issuing stop work orders, blocking permits, and removing tax incentives. We’re still seeing a rush of new solar and wind farms driven by relatively low costs, although many of them make up the last wave of projects that benefited from Biden-era incentives.

The winds are shifting in favor of gas-fired power plants. Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 percent of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 percent by the second quarter of 2026, according to the new report, which analyzes data from the US Energy Information Administration. If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 percent of the development pipeline by the end of the decade. Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 gigawatts by 2030, reflecting a 45 percent jump from construction plans just six months ago.

Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown. But for now, renewable energy projects are being canceled at a faster clip than fossil fuels, at 4.9 percent compared to 2.9 percent of projects, respectively.

New utility-scale solar and wind farms still beat gas when it comes to cost, coming in at $68 to $69 per megawatt-hour on average compared to $90 per megawatt-hour for new combined-cycle natural gas plants, the report finds. Fossil fuels are also subject to increasing price volatility, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran. Gas and coal power plants also emit air pollutants and the greenhouse gases causing climate change, leading to more health costs. Electricity bills have risen across the nation as utilities upgrade power grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.

title: Googlebook will improve support for Linux apps eventually, but it’s all about AI for now
snippet: Googlebook was always going to run into problems with app availability, but few expected the platform to regress its support for Linux apps from Chromebook’s fairly robust solution. In a blog post, Google reiterates that the “Linux Terminal Preview” on Googlebook isn’t for using Linux apps, but for building with AI. more…
fullText:
Googlebook was always going to run into problems with app availability, but few expected the platform to regress its support for Linux apps from Chromebook’s fairly robust solution. In a blog post, Google reiterates that the “Linux Terminal Preview” on Googlebook isn’t for using Linux apps, but for building with AI.

ChromeOS introduced support for Linux apps a few years ago, allowing users to install apps designed for Linux on their machines to expand what the laptops could do. Googlebook does not have this same support, with the Linux Terminal accessible and apps technically installable, but those apps now show up alongside Android and web apps, nor do they feature the same level of user-facing functionality.

In a blog post this week, Google reiterates that the priority around Linux support on Googlebook is, for now, focused on AI-aided app development. 

Today, getting the most out of AI workflows requires access to a terminal with a command line, even if someone doesn’t identify as a programmer or software developer. With Googlebook, we’re excited to help users express themselves and gain access to these tools. Googlebooks come with pre-installed tooling to get you going.

Google says that the Terminal is designed to be the “entry point” for AI agents so that tools like Google’s own Antigravity can use command-line tools within the Linux virtual machine. That setup also ensures your private files are isolated from the agent’s access (unless you grant access). 

	
	

The Linux Terminal implementation on Googlebook is “optimized for rapid prototyping, web development, scripting, and agentic workflows via CLI,” Google says, with a future focus on “building not only on Googlebook but also for your other devices” while also fine-tuning the experience for “heavier workloads.” 

Also directly mentioned is that Google is working on support for showing Linux GUI apps in the app launcher, which is the main downside to the current implementation. 

We can’t wait for the terminal and Linux VM to continue getting more capable over time, including Linux GUI app support with integration directly into the app launcher.

There’s no word on when this might arrive, but the focus right now is very much on AI and development. The rest of Google’s roadmap includes:

We are working hard to get you building not only on Googlebook but also for your other devices. In addition to the existing network passthrough and wireless ADB, USB passthrough and support for ADB over USB are coming, enabling local device debugging and more from our Linux VM and Antigravity. Learn more about Antigravity on Googlebook.

Our testers have been eager to run more complex tasks. To make this more seamless, we are adding dynamic memory and storage scaling for the VM.

We will be adding GPU/NPU hardware acceleration for heavier local workloads, allowing users to leverage the performance and power efficiency of dedicated hardware.

VM persistence and separation from the terminal window will better support long-running processes, when you want to take on more demanding agentic workloads.

title: Seniors Lose More Money to Investment Scams Than Any Other Fraud
snippet: Around $3 billion was lost in 2025 to fraud from people aged 60 and over in the US.
fullText:
Just when older adults need their money for retirement, many of them are being robbed. On Monday, the Federal Trade Commission issued its annual report to Congress on protecting older adults, noting that adults 60 and over continue to report losing far more money to investment scams than to any other type of fraud.

Adults 60 and over lost $3 billion to fraud in 2025, five times the $600 million reported five years prior, in 2020. This increase was driven largely by growing reports of extraordinarily large individual losses. Fraud losses due to investment scams jumped 42% in 2025 to over $1 billion, with consumers reporting that scammers often reach them on social media.

The full 58-page report, Protecting Older Consumers 2025-2026, is available online. It summarizes fraud and consumer complaints submitted to the Consumer Sentinel Network in 2025. The network is a free online investigative FTC tool that gives its member groups access to millions of fraud reports to assist their investigations.

			

More from CNET

Adults 60 and over continue to report much higher individual dollar losses than younger people, with people 80 and over faring the worst, with a median reported loss of $2,000. According to the report, older adults are more likely to report losing money to tech support scams; prize, sweepstakes and lottery scams; romance scams; government impersonation scams; and scams in which someone impersonates their friends or family members.

The government will ‘never ever’ ask for gift cards

The report outlines FTC law enforcement actions targeting fraud aimed at older adults. Those actions include targeted consumer education initiatives and collaboration with government, academic and private-sector partners. The FTC also coordinates with law enforcement and connects victims experiencing significant financial losses to resources such as the Department of Justice’s National Elder Fraud Hotline.

The FTC’s Never Ever campaign, one of those actions, aims to educate seniors by highlighting three red flags that prove a caller or sender is a scammer rather than a legitimate government agency or bank. Those red flags tell people that legitimate government officials will never direct them to transfer money to protect it, threaten to suspend government benefits without immediate payment or demand payment via money apps, cryptocurrency, wire transfers or gift cards.

An article published Monday in PCMag, part of the CNET Group of publications, relays the story of a 77-year-old widow and retired nurse, Mary Ellen Strange, who lost most of her life savings, over $400,000, over a seven-week period in 2024. Strange’s money was taken by a team of cyber scammers led by a man impersonating a Federal Trade Commission officer. On three separate occasions, men pretending to be undercover FBI agents came to her home and left with boxes of her money.

A recent CNET Group survey of 1,000 Americans reveals that scams are a weekly nuisance for many. Over 80% of those surveyed receive scam calls and emails every week, while 76.5% receive weekly scam texts. CNET offers a guide to avoiding the top seven scams, plus tips on how to minimize the damage if you fear you have been scammed.

title: Google support pages start defaulting to AI chatbots – it might be for the best
snippet: Google is starting to move its support pages from detailed articles to AI summaries with a chatbot, with an added set of steps to access the full details of the any given page. more…
fullText:
Google is starting to move its support pages from detailed articles to AI summaries with a chatbot, with an added set of steps to access the full details of the any given page.

The Google Help portal is full of detailed articles that provide step-by-step processes for using a feature, documentation on where features are available or restrictions on them, as well as troubleshooting steps if something goes awry. It’s a massively useful resource, but one that Google is now changing.

Starting with support pages under Google Account Help, the company is shifting these support articles to an AI summary rather than a dedicated article. “Ask Google Help” will display a condensed version of the support article with direct troubleshooting steps, with the user then able to type in queries to have Gemini help figure out the next step forward.

A “View Sources” button at the bottom of the AI response allows users to still access the original article, but direct links to any of these articles now defaults to the AI experience.

	

An example can be seen below on the “Secure a hacked or compromised Google account” page that Google’s own support account directed users to within the past few days. It can also be seen on the “Fix common issues with 2-Step Verification” page and, as far as we can tell, any support pages on the Google Account Help forum.

Google, as of right now, appears to only be testing this on select support topics. The Google Pixel Help section, for instance, still defaults to articles, whereas the Google Chrome topic has also moved to the new experience.

Beyond support pages alone, this new design also impacts the central hub, with links to topics no longer showing by default in exchange for an AI chatbot that helps you find the relevant page.

Ironically enough, the Gemini topic is one of the ones missing this Gemini-powered experience.

9to5Google’s Take

While my initial reaction to this was skeptical, I think this is a rather good use of AI.

Google’s support page collection tends to be a bit of a labyrinth of links and vague search terms. Finding the specific page needed to address the problem you are running into can be very difficult. Meanwhile, Gemini’s inherent ability to understand natural language queries and find associated sources is very powerful in this regard.

I’m still a bit iffy on whether or not dedicated support articles should be converted into an AI summary (which Google still warns could be inaccurate), but using Gemini as a search and troubleshooting tool in this specific regard really highlights a strength of the technology.

What do you think?

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

What’s clear to me from Apple’s bevy of announcements this week is that no one knows how to solve the smart home. The HomeView is the opposite of a home run; the new Apple TV 4K is more than twice the price of its predecessor with little to show for it; the HomePod Mini 2 won’t even ship with Siri AI; and the Apple Home Collection is a collective snore whose products do little to justify their existence.

	

Apple now finds itself pushing the same boulder uphill that Google and Amazon have repeatedly let roll over them for a decade. That is, the smart home is not a singular thing, and even reduced to cameras, light bulbs, locks, and a cavalcade of sensors, its complexity is, for the average person, insurmountable. Some houses may have a couple of Hue lights and a security camera or a water sensor and a smart lock, but the unification of its myriad standards and platforms, even with Matter claiming to solve many of them, still poses many hurdles.

To its credit, Google seems to be righting its own smart home ship at just the right time. While Ben pointed out this week that the Nest Hub hasn’t had a hardware refresh in half a decade, the Gemini-powered platform on which it runs is constantly being improved, and just this week added support to control Hue lights locally over the Matter protocol. 

The move to an LLM-powered smart home hasn’t been smooth for any of the platform owners. Amazon, arguably the early leader in the space, has struggled to gain adoption for its Alexa+ platform. According to The Verge, it “has the memory of a goldfish” and “lacks the personal context a personal assistant needs,” an advantage that Apple and Google share thanks to owning smartphone platforms.

I’d also argue that Google’s first-party Nest hardware isn’t in a bad place, despite its glacial pace of change. The $100 Google Home Speaker is pretty good for the price, and the fourth-generation Nest Learning Thermostat is among the best products the company’s ever made.

With the HomeView, Apple may be going for simplicity over functionality, but in a smart home environment I’m not really sure that’s possible. And even if it does end up selling a boatload of tiny kitchen displays, Google’s in no less strong a position than it was last week. In fact, it may even make the inevitable Google Home Display more compelling.

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Baseus announced a new addition to its lineup of AI-assisted security cameras that’s more proactive about discouraging unwanted visitors instead of just recording and alerting you to their presence. The Baseus Security PrimeSentinel U2 Pro Outdoor 3K Dual Camera introduces a motorized spotlight that shines directly on a moving target, even as they’re running across your property, so they know they’ve been detected. The targeted light also improves the quality of video captured in the dark to increase the chances of a subject being identified, and it can assist your family with after-hours activities like taking the dog out.

The Baseus U2 Pro is now available through Amazon in the US for $269.99, while European availability starts on October 15th at €269.99. Alongside the spotlight feature, the U2 Pro pairs a 3K fixed camera designed to constantly monitor a specific area of your property with a second 3K camera that can zoom, tilt, and pan 360 degrees to monitor everywhere else. Full-color night vision capabilities make it easier to identify people, animals, or even the color of a suspicious vehicle.

Using “AI-powered analysis,” the U2 Pro will provide alerts when motion is detected with summaries and descriptions of what was seen that differentiate between people, pets, vehicles, and activities like delivered packages. It’s also smart enough to ignore movements that aren’t relevant, such as tree branches blowing in the wind, or activities that regularly occur so as not to overwhelm you with notifications. Footage is captured only when motion is detected and is stored locally on a 512GB encrypted memory card. It can be accessed remotely through Baseus’ mobile app, while live views from the cameras can also be monitored on Amazon Alexa or Google Home smart devices.

Baseus claims the U2 Pro can be installed in about two minutes using mounts that connect to walls or ceilings. The camera connects wirelessly to your home network and features a rechargeable battery good for up to 150 days of use, although that will potentially be reduced depending on how much activity there is on your property. An included 3W solar panel can be mounted atop the cameras or a short distance away to ensure it can see the sun. Just 40 minutes of sun exposure generates enough power for a full day’s use.

title: EE announces iPhone Handoff pricing details for UK customers
snippet: As part of its iPhone Duo preorder announcement, UK carrier EE has announced pricing details for iPhone Handoff – making it the first carrier in the UK to do so. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
As part of its iPhone Duo preorder announcement, UK carrier EE has announced pricing details for iPhone Handoff – making it the first carrier in the UK to do so. Here are the details.

At its September keynote, Apple announced iPhone Handoff, a feature that allows users to use their same eSIM across multiple iPhones. It requires support from carriers, and at the keynote, Apple announced T-Mobile, Verizon, EE, and Deutsche Telekom would support it. T-Mobile said it’d be available for $5/month as an add-on for your line, and Verizon just announced it’d be $10/month.

Now, EE is announcing that iPhone Handoff will be available for free as part of its Full Works Plus plan, and available for £5/month on its other plans:

iPhone Handoff allows customers to easily switch back and forth between two iPhone models with the same mobile number. It means customers can choose the iPhone that’s right for the moment, without worrying about missing a call, message or notification.

Whether you’re heading to a festival, going for a run, tackling an all-day hike or simply travelling lighter, your contacts, calls and messages move seamlessly with you.

Included with EE’s Full Works Plus plan which includes Fast Lane, or available for £5 per month on a rolling contract, iPhone Handoff is coming soon and offers a level of flexibility and convenience that isn’t available anywhere else in the UK.

It’s worth noting that it’s still “coming soon,” though Apple did announce that it’ll be available by the end of the year.

title: Blackwall quadruples valuation to $2.2B as websites wrangle an increasingly crowded internet
snippet: Blackwall has raised $100M at a $2.2B valuation to continue building security and filtering tools that help websites grapple with growing bot and AI traffic.
fullText:
Estonia-based Blackwall, which builds web traffic security tools for hosting providers, said on Tuesday that it has raised $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation. It builds products that helps websites grapple with the skyrocketing volume of bot traffic, especially AI agents.

The Series C was led by AVP, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures. Blackwall’s executive chairman, Roi Carthy, told TechCrunch this funding round increased the company’s valuation by 4 times since its previous fundraise in 2025.

Over the past few years, web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva and Blackwall have found themselves in an increasingly valuable but difficult space: They’re on the frontlines, dealing with DDoS attacks, indiscriminate scraping, botnet farms, malicious requests, and these days, even swarms of AI agents going rogue. But it’s also a chance to make a killing by helping hosting providers and websites deal with all the potentially unwanted traffic.

Blackwall, however, isn’t interested in competing with the bigwigs in its space. Instead of selling its platform directly to websites, the company uses a “channel” approach, working with web hosting, managed service and cloud providers to understand their needs, and then handing over a bundle of tools which they can customize. Those providers can then offer Blackwall’s security tools to their own clients under their own branding and retain control of that relationship.

There’s money in it for both sides. Co-founder and CEO Nikita Rozenberg told TechCrunch that hosting companies can mix and match security components to build their own solution according to what they want to provide to their end customers, set the prices, and share a cut of the revenue with Blackwall. The company initially gives its customers a free tier showing the traffic and threats hitting their network, but charges for any protection or tools to address the threats.

In addition to providing services like threat intelligence, certificate management, DDoS protection and traffic routing, Blackwall examines its customers’ web traffic to differentiate actual visitors and legit AI agents from malicious bots, intruders, and disruptive traffic. Rozenberg said the company uses techniques like digital fingerprinting to identify the software sending a request — for example, Microsoft Office or Codex — to filter out bots. In addition, the company uses its own AI models at customers’ endpoints to analyze the intent and behavior of the requests coming in to differentiate agents sent by a person for a real request versus a malicious bot.

In the coming years, Rozenberg sees a big opportunity emerging as AI agents begin interacting and transacting with websites on behalf of their users. This should eventually require systems to manage which agents get access, and on what terms, and how they are authorized to make payments.

Blackwall isn’t alone in eyeing that opportunity. Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control lets website owners allow or block individual AI crawlers, and there’s also an option to charge them for access. But Rozenberg argues that Blackwall’s advantage lies in letting hosting providers offer such traffic management services themselves instead of handing the customer relationship to another security provider.

Blackwall plans to use the funding to expand its operations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, and develop more security tooling for hosting, cloud and managed service providers.

title: MacPaw launches Eney, a proactive AI assistant for Mac and iPhone
snippet: Today marks a milestone for MacPaw, as the company is releasing Eney, a proactive AI assistant that works across your apps, files, and system to help you get things done, following a development process that began back in 2019. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Today marks a milestone for MacPaw, as the company is releasing Eney, a proactive AI assistant that works across your apps, files, and system to help you get things done, following a development process that began back in 2019. Here are the details.

A bit of background

A few days ago, I had the opportunity to talk to Oleksandr Kosovan, founder and CEO of MacPaw, as he showed me Eney, the company’s Mac-first proactive AI assistant.

Eney isn’t a new idea. In fact, we have written about it on 9to5Mac a few times. However, as the underlying AI technology kept changing and evolving, Eney changed and evolved with it.

As Kosovan explained, Eney originated back in 2019 as an idea for simplifying MacPaw’s CleanMyMac through natural-language commands. Then came the LLM boom, which in turn gave way to the agentic AI boom.

More recently, local AI models have become powerful enough to handle increasingly complex tasks that, until not long ago, required much larger cloud-based models.

So, MacPaw kept reworking and refining Eney, which finally launches today for Mac and iPhone.

Here’s MacPaw:

Unlike other AI assistants Eney is built for the Mac: it understands the context of the machine itself — the apps you work across, the files on your disk, the meetings on your calendar — and spots what needs attention before you do. A call about to start. A meeting that needs a summary. A disk running out of space. Eney notices, prepares the next step, and puts it in front of you for approval, without the need to switch between multiple apps, tools and products.

Eney Wand

The very first thing I noticed about Eney was MacPaw’s clever gesture to invoke it through the Eney Wand command. Just shake your cursor over some text, and Eney Wand activates, allowing you to select that text and prompt Eney about it. You can also invoke Eney Wand with the Option + W shortcut, or double-tap the Option key to bring up Eney from anywhere.

The Eney Wand is a particularly clever feature, as it solves one of the main pain points I have with most AI tools: constantly having to copy and paste content in and out of a chat window to get help with whatever I’m working on. Instead, Eney’s system-wide integration lets me simply point to something on my screen and ask the assistant to work with it, without having to move anything between apps.

Eney relies on both local and cloud-based AI models, with MacPaw working alongside Liquid AI to develop custom models optimized for Apple hardware. I recently had the opportunity to visit Liquid AI’s San Francisco headquarters, and it was really impressive to see how the company is bringing advanced AI capabilities to devices that weren’t originally designed to run them. (Not that the Mac isn’t, but you get what I mean, right?)

One of the demonstrations included an AI assistant running on an older Mercedes-Benz, whose hardware was many years old and, at least in theory, nowhere near powerful enough to run modern AI models. But Liquid AI has developed models efficient enough to run on existing hardware with limited computing resources, which goes to show that if one company could help MacPaw with the task of bringing increasingly capable AI models to Macs without relying on the cloud, Liquid AI would be it.

(That doesn’t mean Eney operates entirely on-device, however, as more demanding tasks still rely on cloud-based models.)

Mnemos

Back to Eney, it also relies on Mnemos, MacPaw’s proprietary AI memory system. It allows Eney to remember information about users and their preferences, and use that context to provide more personalized responses and suggestions.

Mnemos uses a knowledge graph to connect information about people, projects, preferences, and events, and it also understands how information changes over time. This means that if you correct something or a previously stored fact becomes outdated, Mnemos can keep track of what is currently relevant and update accordingly.

Another important aspect is privacy. Mnemos is designed to store and process memories locally on the Mac. It also distinguishes between information explicitly provided by the user, facts retrieved from connected sources, and patterns inferred from previous interactions.

However, Mnemos is still in development, and not all of its capabilities are available through Eney just yet. For now, its integration is limited to managing Eney’s own memories, rather than independently accessing information stored in other apps.

During our conversation, Kosovan confirmed that Eney already supports importing ChatGPT archives, which is a great plus for users who want to bring their existing context and preferences into the new assistant.

More ways Eney can help

Another tentpole feature of Eney is its writing assistance tools. As MacPaw explains, the Eney Spell feature “fixes spelling, grammar and wording right in Mail, Slack, Notes or the browser,” and it works very similarly to tools such as Grammarly.

With today’s launch, Eney works in eight languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Polish, Brazilian Portuguese, and Ukrainian. During our demo, Eney occasionally switched between English and Ukrainian, after Kosovan interacted with Eney in Ukrainian. It’s a mistake that won’t seem particularly unusual to frequent users of LLMs and chatbots, and shouldn’t be a dealbreaker for most users.

Beyond these features, Eney is also designed to anticipate what users might need based on what’s happening across their Mac. For example, copying some text can prompt Eney to offer a translation or summary, while an upcoming calendar event can trigger a reminder to prepare for a meeting.

And speaking of meetings, Eney can also transcribe calls without requiring a separate bot to join the conversation, a useful feature for anyone relying on AI-powered meeting summaries. Afterward, Eney can prepare notes, action items, and follow-up invitations for the user to review and approve.

And, in keeping with MacPaw’s roots, Eney also includes some Mac maintenance capabilities. It can warn users about low disk space, memory pressure, and repeatedly crashing apps, suggest possible fixes, organize the Downloads folder, and help locate files.

Eney also includes ready-made workflows such as Morning Brief, Plan My Day, and Weekly Review, which can be triggered manually or scheduled to run automatically.

To make all of this possible, Eney integrates with a wide range of apps and services. It works with Apple Mail, Calendar, and Reminders out of the box, and also supports connections to Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Slack, Notion, Jira, Linear, and more.

The idea is to let users work across these services through a single interface, without constantly switching between apps or manually transferring information from one to another.

Availability

Eney launches today on the Mac, and you can get it here. Eney offers a 14-day free trial with 10,000 AI credits, after which users can choose from three subscription plans: Starter, with 10,000 monthly credits for $14.99; Boost, with 20,000 credits for $29.99; and Power, with 30,000 credits for $49.99.

Users can also sign in with a Setapp account. Importantly, a Setapp membership isn’t required, but something tells me Eney might become even more useful in the future as MacPaw expands its integration with the apps available through Setapp. That is certainly where I would go next.

title: Samsung’s first Android XR glasses leak in 25 styles alongside 9-hour battery, specs [Gallery]
snippet: Samsung’s first Android XR glasses are right around the corner and, ahead of launch, another leak reveals every style you’ll be able to buy. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s first Android XR glasses are right around the corner and, ahead of launch, another leak reveals every style you’ll be able to buy. 

SammyGuru uncovered a bunch of new details around Samsung’s first Android XR glasses this week including the key specs. While it varies by style, Samsung’s glasses will weigh as little as 41g, over 10g lighter than the nearest Ray-Ban Meta glasses with a camera, and still lighter than the new audio-only styles by a couple of grams.

Powering Samsung’s Android XR glasses you’ll find:

Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 chip

2GB of RAM

64GB of storage

9-hour battery (72 hours with case)

12MP camera: 3K video, 30fps

Two speakers, four microphones

The battery life and cameras match the latest generation of Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

	

On the compatibility side, Samsung’s Android XR glasses will have basic functionality across Android phones and iPhone, but certain Galaxy-only features require One UI 9 (Android 17) on your phone and Wear OS 7 on Galaxy Watch.

As far as styles go, Samsung’s partnerships with Gentle Monster and Warby Parker are set to deliver a lot of different choices. There are three frame styles from Warby Parker – Alden (rounded), Reid (square-ish), and Wren (cateye-ish).

Meanwhile, Gentle Monster has six frame styles ranging from rectangular to a slim oval. 

Both brands have different color options for the frames and the lenses, with Warby Parker having black, brown, and green colors, but Gentle Monster offering a lot more with gray, purple, burgundy, brown, and other color options to pick from.

title: Meta Blames Bot Traffic for No Kings Day Instagram Suspension
snippet: The No Kings Coalition says that even after the account was visible again, they couldn’t access it for hours.
fullText:
Meta, the owner of Instagram, apologized for disabling an Instagram account run by No Kings Coalition, the organizers of the No Kings Day political rallies held across the country on Oct. 17.

Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, posted about the events on X the day of the rallies, with a follow-up message the next day. Stone said the blackout lasted about an hour in the middle of the protests and was an accidental shutdown caused by the engineering team’s automated systems detecting a traffic spike.

Specifically, the team detected a Claude AI tool reading profiles, posts and hashtags at an unusually high rate.

			

More from CNET

“It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account,” Stone wrote.

A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.

The timing and duration of the outage were criticized by the No Kings Coalition, which wrote about it on the restored account.

“Even after visibility was restored, we still had no access to the account for hours,” the post read. “Meta still owes us an explanation. Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”

As of Monday afternoon, the Instagram post had more than 70,000 likes. A representative for the No Kings Coalition did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Saturday’s rallies took place a year after the group’s 2025 events, when protests were organized in 2,500 cities. The rallies, which began in June of last year, protest the policies of President Donald Trump. This year, the impending Nov. 3 midterm elections have added urgency to the events, with demonstrations focused on educating voters about early voting and expanding voter registration.

“The public is clearly primed to suspect that platforms’ high-profile content moderation decisions are politically motivated,” said Kate Ruane, director of the Free Expression Project at the nonprofit Center for Democracy & Technology, in an email.

Ruane noted that the automated moderation tools Meta blamed for the removal of the account have “important limitations including poor performance when making context-dependent decisions, especially for real-time and fast-moving events,” she said. “Users deserve to know when their content and accounts are being taken down and why, regardless of moderation method.”

Activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, who said she was at a No Kings Coalition event in Dallas over the weekend, accused Meta of disrupting other accounts in the past during other political activism events. 

“You mean to tell me in the middle of that day, it just so happens that the No Kings account is down for almost two hours?” she said in an Instagram video response. “I’ve got questions, and somebody needs to have some answers.”

Meta is also dealing with blowback about a separate issue. The company backtracked on plans to change its contractual language for business customers in a way that would have allowed it to scrape information for AI training.
